questions.question: How do the `os`, `io`, and `bufio` packages fit together?
questions.title: The os, io, and bufio layers
questions.direct_answer: `os` opens files and exposes operating-system resources such as `*os.File`. `io` defines shared stream interfaces and transfer helpers. `bufio` wraps Readers and Writers to add buffering and token-oriented operations. Typical code opens with os, processes through io or bufio abstractions, then flushes and closes at the owning boundary.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `io` supplies Reader, Writer, and composition helpers.
`bufio` adds buffers, line/token scanning, and delimiter methods.
One `*os.File` can satisfy both Reader and Writer contracts when opened accordingly.
The layer that creates wrappers must complete Flush and Close in order.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The packages solve different layers of one I/O problem. `os` deals with names, flags, permissions, environment state, and concrete `*os.File` handles. It is where a local file resource is acquired and later closed.

`io` supplies the small Reader and Writer contracts plus helpers such as Copy, ReadAll, LimitReader, and MultiWriter. Code written at this layer can process a file, network body, compression stream, or memory buffer without depending on the concrete source.

`bufio` decorates those interfaces with an in-memory buffer. Scanner turns a Reader into bounded tokens, Reader adds delimiter-oriented methods, and Writer combines small output calls. For example, a file from os can be wrapped in Scanner to count lines and still be passed wherever an io.Reader is expected.

The abstractions do not erase ownership. The code that opens the file closes it; the code that creates a buffered writer flushes it before close. I choose the lowest layer that expresses the algorithm and keep os-specific lifecycle at the application's boundary.

sections.title: Concrete resource outside, small capability inside
sections.content:
A common design opens a concrete resource at the edge, passes an interface into processing code, and decorates it only where buffering or tokenisation is useful. This keeps core logic reusable while the edge retains lifecycle control.

The direction also makes tests simple: replace the os.File endpoint with strings.Reader or bytes.Buffer without changing the transformation. Only the thin resource-opening layer needs filesystem tests.

sections.title: Wrappers add behaviour without changing the stream boundary
sections.content:
`bufio.Reader` remains an io.Reader and `bufio.Writer` remains an io.Writer. The wrapper can therefore participate in other io helpers, although its additional state means callers must not bypass or reorder operations carelessly.

Opening mode still limits capability. A file opened with `os.Open` can satisfy Reader but writes fail; a file from `os.Create` is opened read-write but has already truncated old content. Interface compatibility does not override the concrete resource policy chosen at acquisition.

sections.title: A layered file-processing pipeline
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[os.Open returns *os.File] --> B[io.Reader boundary]
  B --> C[bufio.Scanner adds lines]
  C --> D[application processing]
  D --> E[bufio.Writer adds batching]
  E --> F[io.Writer destination]
  F --> G[Flush then os.File.Close]
```

questions.question: When should you use `os.ReadFile`, `bufio.Scanner`, or `io.Copy`?
questions.title: Choosing a file-reading shape
questions.direct_answer: Use `os.ReadFile` when a bounded file must become one byte slice, `bufio.Scanner` when bounded text tokens such as lines should be handled one at a time, and `io.Copy` when bytes should move from a Reader to a Writer without interpretation. Choose by memory shape, record boundaries, and whether the application must inspect the content.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: ReadFile returns the complete file as one byte slice.
Scanner exposes bounded tokens and requires a final Err check.
Copy transfers bytes without interpreting records.
Total file size and maximum token size are different limits.
The caller owns files and partial-output policy in streaming paths.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`os.ReadFile` is the simplest shape when the complete content is small and bounded. It is a good fit for configuration, templates, and test fixtures that genuinely need one byte slice. Its memory grows with total file size.

`bufio.Scanner` is for token-based processing. With the default split it reads lines incrementally, which suits logs and text imports. The total file may be large, but every token must fit the configured Scanner limit and `Err` must be checked after the loop.

`io.Copy` is for uninterpreted transfer. For example, copying an upload to storage does not require the application to split lines or hold all bytes. Copy streams between interfaces, reports progress and failure, and may use endpoint-specific fast paths.

I decide whether the algorithm needs one complete value, individual records, or only transport. Then I state the size boundary and ownership policy. Using Scanner for arbitrary binary bytes, ReadFile for an unbounded upload, or Copy when each record needs validation gives the wrong abstraction even if the code compiles.

sections.title: Concept guide · Choosing a file-reading shape
sections.content:
Representation follows the next step. A parser that needs random access benefits from one complete slice; a line validator benefits from tokens; a relay benefits from leaving the stream uninterpreted.

Each choice has a separate failure boundary. ReadFile can fail after partial internal work but returns no partial slice contract, Scanner can stop on a token error, and Copy can leave the destination with a reported partial byte count.

sections.title: Do not select an API from file size alone
sections.content:
A small binary file may still be better as ReadFile, while a modest CSV needs Scanner because records drive validation. A large format that requires random access may need a different design such as memory mapping, indexing, or a format-specific streaming parser rather than blindly selecting one of these three.

Boundedness should come from a real source: deployment-controlled config limit, HTTP body limit, database field maximum, or protocol definition. Without that contract, convenience can turn into an availability problem under unexpected input.

sections.title: Select by data shape
sections.content:
| Need | Tool | Memory driver | Interprets records? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Complete bounded value | `os.ReadFile` | Entire file | No |
| One bounded text token at a time | `bufio.Scanner` | Largest token | Yes, through split function |
| Transfer bytes to another endpoint | `io.Copy` | Transfer buffer / fast path | No |

questions.question: How do you make Go I/O code easy to test without real files?
questions.title: Testing I/O through Reader and Writer
questions.direct_answer: Put parsing or transformation logic in a function that accepts `io.Reader` and `io.Writer`, then test it with `strings.Reader`, `bytes.Buffer`, and small fault-injecting implementations. Keep path opening, permissions, and cleanup in a thin outer function. This makes core tests fast and deterministic while preserving a few focused filesystem integration tests.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Accept Reader and Writer at the algorithm boundary.
Use strings.Reader or bytes.Reader for deterministic input.
Use bytes.Buffer to capture and assert output.
Use small custom implementations to inject read, write, or short-write failures.
Test path and permission behaviour separately at the os boundary.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
File handling and content processing are different responsibilities. I keep `os.Open`, flags, path validation, and Close in a thin boundary, then pass the opened stream to a function that depends only on `io.Reader` and `io.Writer`.

Unit tests can supply `strings.NewReader` or `bytes.NewReader` and capture output in `bytes.Buffer`. They run without temporary paths, platform permissions, or cleanup. A tiny custom Reader or Writer can return a planned error, final data with EOF, or a short write to cover branches that real files rarely reproduce reliably.

For example, a `numberLines(dst, src)` function can scan two in-memory lines and write numbered output to a buffer. The test compares one string. Production can call the same function with an input file and output file because both satisfy the interfaces.

Not every test should avoid the filesystem. A smaller integration layer should still verify opening flags, creation modes, root containment, rename behaviour, and close ordering on supported platforms. Interface tests prove transformation semantics; filesystem tests prove the concrete resource boundary.

sections.title: Move nondeterminism to a thin edge
sections.content:
The operating system introduces names, permissions, timing, disk state, and platform differences. Most parsing and formatting logic needs none of those. Interfaces let tests replace only the byte endpoints while exercising the real algorithm.

Fault-injecting types are often clearer than mocks. A few lines implementing Read or Write can model an exact partial result and error, directly matching the standard contract the production code must handle.

sections.title: Concept guide · Testing I/O through Reader and Writer
sections.content:
Unit tests cover content cases: empty input, malformed records, Unicode, final lines without newlines, read failure, write failure, and short write. They can run in parallel when all state is local.

Integration tests cover resource cases: missing parent directories, existing-file truncation, requested modes under platform policy, confined path access, and cleanup. `t.TempDir` gives each test an automatically removed directory, but environment mutation and other process-wide settings still require separate care.

sections.title: One core function, two endpoint sets
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[strings.Reader in unit test] --> C[numberLines Reader, Writer]
  B[os.File in production] --> C
  C --> D[bytes.Buffer in unit test]
  C --> E[os.File in production]
  F[thin os boundary] -. opens and closes .-> B
  F -. opens and closes .-> E
```
